_note: Style presets, ported from the old tool's niche_styles.json.
niche     - subject matter and tone (WW2 History, True Crime, Relationship Advice)
art_style - how the picture is rendered (Studio Ghibli Style, Pixar 3D, Chibi Cute)
style - the STYLE: line in the agent prompt (story_to_agent_prompt.js)
whisk - wording for character-sheet / image prompts, used by hand in Whisk
The rest - palette, camera, audience - are authoring notes for a human. No tool
`label` MAY NAME A REAL STUDIO. `style` and `whisk` MUST NOT.
The label is a menu entry; the other two are typed into a prompt. Naming a real
studio or brand is a distinctive protected house style, and Google's models
often refuse or quietly sanitise such prompts. The Bridge story had to be
rewritten to remove 27 mentions of one studio name for exactly this reason, so
the presets describe the look instead. Label 'Studio Ghibli Style' is how you
find the entry; its `style` says 'hand-painted 2D animation, soft watercolour
backgrounds' and never uses the word. Swap a label's wording into `style`
yourself if you would rather name the studio and take the risk.

styles.label: Fern Documentary Style
styles.style: Stylised cinematic 3D documentary reconstruction. Every human is an unmistakable smooth faceless mannequin with a completely blank matte head: no eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, ears, skin pores or hair. Realistic adult proportions and simple role-appropriate clothing. Modelled 3D aircraft and environments, desaturated slate and teal with warm highlights, physically grounded cinematic lighting. Never live-action people or photorealistic human faces.
styles.whisk: Stylised 3D documentary render, smooth completely faceless matte mannequin people, role-appropriate simple clothing, modelled 3D environments, desaturated teal and slate cinematic lighting; no human facial features or hair.
styles.palette: Teal shadows, warm orange highlights, desaturated blues
styles.camera: Each eight-second clip contains two or three distinct documentary shots linked to the narration: an establishing view, a detail or diagram, and a consequence or wider context. Specify shot timings totalling exactly eight seconds, e.g. 0-3s, 3-5.5s, 5.5-8s. Use clear editorial cuts within the same output clip, with restrained camera movement inside each shot. Not one continuous slow pan.
styles.audience: Psychology fans, deep thinkers, documentary lovers
story_shapes: a philosophical question explored through one silent life
a solitary figure observed across decades
a place that remembers the people who left it
styles.narration_voice: soft measured male voice, contemplative and slow, almost melancholy
styles.avoid: no live-action footage, no photorealistic human faces or skin, no eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, ears or hair on mannequin heads, no character dialogue or lip movement, no gore, no long static single-shot clips, no random shots unrelated to narration, no extra output clips for internal shots, no bright saturated palette
styles.cast_idiom: A stylised 3D mannequin with a completely smooth blank matte head and realistic adult proportions. No eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, ears, hair or photorealistic skin. Simple role-appropriate clothing, fixed materials and proportions across shots.
styles.direction: FACeless 3D documentary reconstruction: EVERY person, including background passengers and crew, must be a smooth blank-headed mannequin, never a realistic human. Narration is voice-over; all figures remain silent. Plan TWO OR THREE visible shots WITHIN EACH eight-second video clip, matched to the successive phrases actually spoken in that clip. Write explicit SHOT 1 (0-3s), SHOT 2 (3-5.5s), SHOT 3 (5.5-8s), or two shots when the narration has only two visual ideas. Each shot must depict the corresponding narration, rather than unrelated events from another part of the story. Keep one uninterrupted voice-over across the internal cuts. These internal shots are NOT additional scenes or output clips. Preserve the requested total clip count and cover the entire source. Use a factual documentary delivery, clear normal volume, no character speech. Sets can change as the narrated events require; do not force every event into one room.

styles.direction: Ground every animal in real behaviour - head turns, ear tilts, weight shifts, shivering, a vigilant stance, cautious hesitation. An animal is never a passive prop and never behaves like a person. Humans are ordinary and tired, never villains and never saints. Put a hook - a visual anomaly or a striking emotional beat - inside the first two seconds. Deliver the lesson through action and through what it costs, never by saying it.

styles.direction: Every clip is an evolving geographic VISUALISATION, not a flat slide: glowing boundaries, dashed tracer lines with animated chevron arrows, and translucent illuminated polygon fills demonstrate the single factual claim the narrator is voicing at that instant. Frame ONE already contains the anomaly: the surprising visualisation is happening in the first second - never a slow map tour, a zoom-out to establish, or any build-up. Clip 1 is a HOOK and never the first fact: lead with the single most counter-intuitive claim as a flat STATEMENT, not a question (a question is only the fallback). Every clip after carries exactly ONE new fact or deduction with its specifics (a length, a year, a country, a number) and never repeats the previous line. The last clip is the biggest revelation and its final frame visually echoes the first frame so the film loops. Show the fact, never narrate a walkthrough. Exaggerate every instruction - the model treats 'moves' as 'barely moves': say fast, aggressive, big dramatic framing change, never static. Numbers are spoken as words ('seven thousand', not '7,000'). ENGAGEMENT ICONS (one general rule, never per-topic): as the narrator voices each line, small flat emoji-style icons / sticker graphics pop in on the map, timed to the exact moment each concrete thing is named or implied. Match the icon to whatever the sentence is about - a country or city gets its flag or a simple map-pin marker, war or battle gets crossed swords / a rifle / a tank / a fighter-jet / an explosion burst, money gets a coin or a stack of cash, a ship or voyage gets a ship, a treaty or document gets a scroll, a person or role gets a small flat avatar silhouette, terrain or nature gets a mountain, river, tree or wave, and so on for any noun the line carries. Keep ONE consistent cartoony sticker language for the whole film (thick dark outline, flat fill, soft drop shadow), each icon pops in with a punchy scale-up, each sits beside the relevant point on the map, none covers the map's key line or highlighted border, and none contains any text. No people, no talking heads, no on-screen text.

styles.camera: Strong continuous movement in every shot, built as TWO OR THREE TIMED BEATS that together cover the clip's whole duration. Write those beats into the scene as explicit time ranges - for an 8-second clip, 0-3s, 3-6s, 6-8s. Each beat names what the camera is on, what changes, and how it hands over to the next: a fast push-in, a hard framing change, a whip-pan, a rack focus, a see-through transition. There is never a dead or static moment anywhere in the clip. Strong multi-plane 3D PARALLAX in every move, so foreground, subject and background slide against each other and the depth reads as real depth rather than a flat image drifting. Start on A then push in fast and hard onto B with a slight arc. Kinetic and exaggerated, never static, never a subtle drift. One clear idea per shot.
styles.direction: SOURCE-FAITHFUL RETELLING WITH A HOOK AND AN EXTRA CTA. When a reference video, transcript or source script is supplied, first understand who did what, with which objects, in which order, and how the story ended. Preserve every material event, cause, outcome, number and qualification. Rewrite the wording in easy, natural English without copying whole sentences. Keep the original viewpoint and tense: a past event about he or she stays a past event about that person, never advice beginning "you can". Do not invent quantities, upgrades, explanations, motives or capabilities. An object described as stab-proof must never become bulletproof. OPENING: make the first source event arresting through concise wording and a strong moving image, without moving later events forward or inventing a claim. BODY: retell the source events in their original sequence, with no added facts and no skipped ending. ENDING: finish the original outcome completely in the last STORY clip. THEN append one separate extra CTA clip, with no new story event and no replacement of the ending. The extra CTA is the only place to address the viewer directly. Existing visual style, bright cyan-blue presentation, moving camera and clean cutaways remain visual treatment, never permission to change the facts. When only an original idea is supplied, write a coherent original story using the same opening, story, ending, extra CTA structure.
styles.hook_line: Open cold on the single most shocking image supported by the FIRST source event. Make that first event immediately interesting with simple, punchy wording; never a walk-in, never a greeting, never a fabricated number or claim. Preserve the subject and tense. Do not turn "he did" into "you can", do not reveal a later outcome early, and do not suppress the first event merely to create mystery. The hook is part of the first story clip, not a replacement for the original story.
styles.ask_line: This EXTRA clip follows the complete original ending, and it is required. It is the only clip allowed to break the fourth wall. ONE short warm sentence asks the viewer a relevant question about the story. This is NOT the hard sell the NEVER list forbids. Do not add a new event, repeat the whole ending, or combine the final source fact with the CTA. Keep the camera moving on an already established subject; no title card or invented aftermath.

styles.direction:
FIXED COUPLE NAMES: The woman is always Sarah and the man is always George. Never keep the source video couple names. Replace those names everywhere: cast, speaker labels, spoken lines (including direct address), outline, visual descriptions, blocking and reference sheet prompts. Name replacement is mandatory and overrides word-retention rules; preserve the same meaning and speaker roles. SOURCE VIDEO DIALOGUE RULE: When a reference video or transcript is supplied, its conversation is ground truth. Keep the same speakers, turn order, questions, answers, sentence meaning, conflict and ending. Never replace it with a newly invented relationship script. Use only a light English simplification: in a ten-word source line, change no more than about three words, and only to easier words with the same meaning. Preserve at least seventy percent of the words in every line and virtually all of the dialogue structure. If the source line is already simple, copy it exactly. Do not add dialogue merely to make both people speak in every clip; follow the source clip's actual turns. This source rule overrides the original-story structure below. GROUNDED RESPECTFUL TWO-PERSON RELATIONSHIP CONVERSATION. Exactly two adults share one private, believable room and discuss one specific relationship problem in normal voices. The same room, light, time of day, faces, hair, clothing, jewellery and fixed seating remain unchanged for the whole film. There is no narrator: every word is spoken naturally by one person to the other. Start in the middle of the real issue with one concise line that creates emotional curiosity without shouting, accusation bait or manufactured drama. Let both people have an understandable point of view. Build the conversation through listening, clarification, a concrete example, the vulnerable reason underneath the conflict, respectful disagreement, recognition of impact, and a specific boundary, apology, question or next step. Use plain conversational English, contractions, incomplete thoughts and short pauses. Nobody delivers a speech, numbered advice list, moral lesson or therapist monologue. They do not describe what the viewer can see. Emotion stays controlled but readable through a pause, swallowed reply, tightened hand, softened eyes, shifted breath or careful choice of words. No one is purely right, evil, miraculously transformed or rewarded by fate. The ending may be warm, cautious or unresolved, but it must feel emotionally earned and leave the relationship in a clearer place. One person speaks while the other genuinely listens and reacts; avoid talking over each other except for one brief natural interruption when the story requires it. For an original idea with no source dialogue, every 8-second clip is an active back-and-forth: both people speak at least once, using two or three turns and 18-24 spoken words total. When source dialogue is supplied, its actual turns and length override this density target. Speech starts within the first half-second and naturally occupies six to seven seconds while the listener reacts. Never write a one-line clip, a long silent tail, padded greetings, repeated thoughts or filler.
SPEAKER IDENTITY: Sarah is always the female source speaker; George is always the male source speaker. Identify the source speaker from matching voice, visible mouth movements, and stable identity before rewriting. Never assign lines from cast order, alternating turn assumptions, question/answer roles, sentence meaning or stereotypes. Preserve every source turn and its gender. Consecutive turns can belong to the same person. For pasted text require Female: / Male: or Sarah: / George: labels on every turn. Unknown or conflicting gender must be flagged for review, never guessed. Sarah uses her own female voice; George uses his own male voice. Only the named speaker moves their lips.
styles.blocking: SPATIAL BLOCKING (LOCKED): exactly two adults remain in the same private room and on the same seats or standing marks chosen in clip 1. Person A stays screen-left in every wide two-shot; Person B stays screen-right. The camera remains on one side of the 180-degree axis, so over-the-shoulder angles may change the frame emphasis but never reverse their real positions. Nobody walks around, changes seats, enters, exits, paces, embraces or touches the other unless the story explicitly earns one small action in the final beat. Faces, hairstyle, clothing, jewellery, props, furniture, lighting and time of day never change. Keep gestures small and human: fingers tightening around a cup, hands uncurling, a breath held, eye contact broken and restored, shoulders easing. Each listener remains visibly present and reacts while the other speaks.
